In the present batch of matters, the petitioners have  sought for quashing of the entire criminal prosecution initiated  against them solely on the ground that they have been exonerated in  the departmental proceeding initiated against them on the selfsame  allegations, hence, the prosecution cannot proceed with the criminal  Page 4 of 30  cases against them.

The common question of law regarding the  applicability of the judgments of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the  fact scenario of the present cases is the point of determination in the  present batch of cases.
Therefore, all the matters are heard  analogously and by a common judgment, they are disposed of.
Bereft of unnecessary details the facts of all the cases in  brevity are enumerated as preface to the Judgement.

Learned Senior Counsel for the petitioners further submitted that similar issue was again in consideration before a three Judge Bench in the case of Ajay Kumar Tyagi (supra) of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in which the Court held as under:
 "25.
We are, therefore, of the opinion that the exoneration  in the departmental proceeding ipso facto would not result  in the quashing of the criminal prosecution.
We hasten to  add, however, that if the prosecution against an accused is  solely based on a finding in a proceeding and that finding  is set aside by the superior authority in the hierarchy
, the  very foundation goes and the prosecution may be quashed.
Page 15 of 30
But that principle will not apply in the case of the  departmental proceeding as the criminal trial and the  departmental proceeding are held by two different entities.
Further, they are not in the same hierarchy."

However, the petitioners' counsel contended that in t aforementioned judgment, the Hon'ble Court has not noticed the prior ruling in Radheyshyam Kejriwal (supra) by a coordinate Bench of three Judges, which decided the same issue differently.
Although, the Senior Counsel is not being questioning the judgment of Ajay Kumar Tyagi (supra) in terms of its authority, it is argued that the former should be considered per incuriam.

sentences.text: The Petitioners place their reliance on the judgment in Ashoo Surendranath Tewari (supra) for two key reasons.
First, it properly acknowledges the prior decision of a coordinate Bench in Radheyshyam Kejriwal (supra) on the same issue, in line with judicial propriety and discipline.

No Supreme Court decision by a Bench of three or more Judges has contradicted it, making Ashoo Surendranath Tewari (supra)
the latest authoritative ruling on the matter.

We are in respectful agreement with the above view.
The purpose of departmental enquiry and of prosecution are two different and distinct aspects.

The criminal prosecution is launched for an offence for violation of a duty, the offender owes to the society or for breach of which law has provided that the offender shall make satisfaction to the public.
So crime is an act of commission in violation of law or of omission of public duty.
The departmental enquiry is to maintain discipline in the service and efficiency of public service.
It would, therefore, be expedient that the disciplinary proceedings are conducted and completed as expeditiously as possible.

It is not, therefore, desirable to lay down any guidelines as inflexible rules in which the departmental proceedings may or may not be stayed pending trial in criminal case against the delinquent officer.
Each case requires to be considered in the backdrop of its own facts and circumstances.

sentences.text: Converse is the case of departmental enquiry.
The enquiry in a departmental proceedings relates to conduct or breach of duty of the delinquent officer to punish him for his misconduct defined under the relevant statutory rules or law.
That the strict standard of proof or applicability of the Evidence Act stands excluded is a settled legal position.
The enquiry in the departmental proceedings relates to the conduct of the delinquent officer and proof in that behalf is not as high as in an offence in criminal charge.
It is seen that invariably the departmental enquiry has to be conducted expeditiously so as to effectuate efficiency in public administration and the criminal trial will take its own course.
The nature of evidence in criminal trial is entirely different from the departmental proceedings.
In the former, prosecution is to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt on the touchstone of human conduct.
The standard of proof in the departmental proceedings is not the same as of the criminal trial.
The evidence also is different from the standard point of the Evidence Act.
The evidence required in the departmental enquiry is not regulated by the Evidence Act.
Under these circumstances, what is required to be seen is whether the departmental enquiry would seriously prejudice the delinquent in his defence at the trial in a criminal case.
It is always a question of fact to be considered in each case depending on its own facts and circumstances.
In this case, we have seen that the charge is failure to anticipate the accident and prevention thereof.
It has nothing to do with the culpability of the offence under Sections 304-A and 338, IPC.
Under these circumstances, the High Court was not right in staying the proceedings."

Additionally, while the judgment in Ajay Tyagi (supra) specifically addresses departmental proceedings, the subsequent decision in Ashoo Surendranath (supra) did not rely on the ratio of Ajay Tyagi (supra) (a three-judge bench decision) but instead referred to the rulings in P.S. Rajya (supra) (a two-judge bench decision) and Radheshyam Kejriwal (supra), which may not be directly relevant to the issue under consideration.
26.
The rival submission of the learned counsels appearing for the parties prompt this Court to delve upon the distinguishable elements between the departmental and adjudicative proceedings.

The key difference lies on the very nature of proceeding, departmental proceeding aims to the disciplinary purpose of a delinquent officer on the basis of service rules and regulations which is an administrative action whereas adjudication proceeding by its nature involves adjudication by a Quasi-Judicial Authority.
It determines the guilt of the persons facing the proceeding culminating into penalty order.

Therefore, the departmental proceeding deals with service related misconduct within an organization while adjudication proceedings involve a legal dispute resolution process conducted by an independent authority under statutory law.
The law is no longer res integra that "there is distinction between the procedure, purpose and finding of adjudication proceeding and departmental proceeding."
Adjudication proceedings are conducted by statutory bodies under the Act, tribunals, or quasi-judicial authorities, adhering to procedures akin to a formal trial.
In contrast, departmental proceedings are inquiries conducted by departmental authorities, distinct in their purpose and methodology from adjudicatory processes.

Therefore the attempt of the learned Senior Counsel for the petitioners to draw parallel between the departmental proceeding with adjudication proceeding is misconceived.

Hence, exoneration in the departmental proceeding which is the culmination of much lower standard of prove cannot enure to the advantage of the petitioners which would lead to quashing of the criminal proceeding.

Minaketan (supra).

I have carefully evaluated the judgment in Dr. Minaketan (supra), in which the coordinate Bench of this Court has only borrowed the reasoning of Radheshyam Kejriwal (supra) and quashed the proceedings.

Moreover, in Dr. Minaketan (supra) the exoneration in departmental proceeding had undergone judicial scrutiny by the Orissa Administrative Tribunal (OAT) and then by this Court in W.P.(C) No. 2225 of 2015 which was dismissed 19.12.2017.
Again an S.L.P. was filed before Hon'ble Supreme Court being SLP (Civil) No.23691 of 2018, which came to be dismissed on 19.07.2019.

Therefore the coordinate Bench of this Court by adopting the reasoning of the decision of Radheshyam (supra) granted benefit of departmental exoneration to the delinquent officer and quash criminal prosecution qua him.
Hence, the judgment of the coordinate Bench of this Court in Dr. Minaketan (supra) is clearly distinguishable and does not lay down subtle ratio as propounded by the petitioners herewith.

30. It is further noteworthy to mention that in all the cases under consideration, notwithstanding the exoneration of petitioners in departmental proceedings, the competent authority on evaluation of the materials on record accorded sanction to prosecute the petitioners.

After grant of sanction by the competent authority, the effect of exoneration in departmental proceedings loses its sanctity because the sanctioning authority accords sanction to prosecute the accused on the material placed before him which form the part of the charge sheet and arrived at the satisfaction that prima facie materials are there against the public servant which warrant prosecution.

The P.C. Act is special statute and this Act is enacted keeping in view to curtail the rampant corruption by the public servants.
The corruption in our country not only possesses a grave danger to the constitution of governance, it is also threatens the very foundation of Indian democracy under Rule of Law.
The magnitude of corruption coming to the liability has all potential to choke the development of the nation and undermines the Rule of Law.
Therefore, it is the duty of the Court to interpret the corruption law to strengthen the fight against corruption.

(1984) 2 SCC 183 a) The standard of proof in the departmental proceedings being preponderance of probability cannot be equated with the standard of proof required in a criminal prosecution.

b) The exoneration of the petitioners in the departmental proceedings shall not enure to the benefit of public servant who is facing charges of PC Act, 1988, which would lead to quashing of the entire criminal prosecution.

g) The judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Ajay Tyagi (supra) passed in 2012 by three Judge Bench supersedes the ratio laid down by the Division Bench of Supreme Court in PS Rajya (supra) in 1996.

h) The exoneration of accused in a departmental proceeding shall have limited bearing in regard to the offences under special statute however, diminish the effect once the sanction for prosecution under special statutes is granted.

33. Therefore, in light of the aforementioned discussion and judgements cited, this Court is of the considered view that there exists a fundamental distinction between adjudication proceedings and departmental proceedings.
